items.t: Vessev built an electric ferry that almost flies
items.d: Vessev hopes its electric hydrofoil ferry will change the way people and cities think about boats.
items.fullText: “When will we start flying?” I asked Vessev co-founder and CEO Eric Laakmann, as we pulled away from the Brooklyn marina in the startup’s VS-9 electric ferry. “We already are.” I’ll admit I was a bit disappointed. I thought the moment when it transitioned from sailing like a regular boat to almost-flying as a surface-skimming hydrofoil would be more … momentous. I’ve been on my share of boats, including large ferries, small sailboats, and plenty of others in between, but never been on a hydrofoil and I was curious what flying along the water might feel like during the brief ride from the Brooklyn Marina out toward Governors Island on the East River in New York. It didn’t feel like flying, but it was a bit like a riding in a sports car. The wake when foiling in the VS-9 is minimal. Image Credits: Tim De Chant/TechCrunch Traditional boats of this size — about 30 feet — start to bounce and slap the water as they gain speed. But on a hydrofoil, that’s when the foils start to do their work. On the surface, the VS-9 looks like plenty of other catamarans. But under the hull are two wing-like structures that lift the boat as they slice through the water. Computer-controlled underwater flaps keep the ride smooth and stable. In the VS-9, most of the lifting is done by the front foil, with about 20% handled by the rear. The VS-9 can raise its foils to access docks in shallower waters. Image Credits: Tim De Chant/TechCrunch The rear foil also hosts the electric motor, which Vessev makes in-house. Why not outsource it? Laakmann said that it’s important to keep costs in line — eventually, you’ll have to bring production in house, so why not do it earlier in development? The only thing Vessev doesn’t build are the batteries. “Those have been commoditized,” Laakmann said. By lifting the hull clear of the water, hydrofoils can operate more efficiently than other boats. items.t: All the AI agents that can live in your text messages
items.d: We created a list of the most notable AI agents that can live in your text messages, from general assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
items.fullText: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are some of the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Caddy Image Credits: Caddy Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot Image Credits: Fambot Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS.

items.t: Sean Parker is rebuilding Stability AI around music
items.d: Sean Parker, who once taught the music industry what asking for forgiveness looks like, is now back with the labels' blessing and money.
items.fullText: In Brief Posted: 2:09 PM PDT · October 2, 2026 Image Credits: Gilbert Carrasquillo / Getty Images Connie Loizos Sean Parker is rebuilding Stability AI around music Sean Parker, the Napster co-founder, has jumped back into the music industry, and he tells The Information that he’s playing by the rules this time. (Asking for forgiveness rather than permission didn’t work out so well last time around, he readily concedes.) Two years ago, he joined an $80 million rescue of Stability AI, the image-generator startup that nearly collapsed after overspending and internal turmoil led to founder Emad Mostaque’s ouster. Now Parker and his longtime friend Prem Akkaraju, who became CEO, are taking the wraps off what they’ve been building. The big idea, Parker says, is to turn Stability into the go-to AI toolmaker for music professionals. Toward that end, in late August, the company announced $76 million in funding from, among others, Sony, Warner, and Universal, which also licensed their catalogs for training as part of the deal. Stability has since released three new audio models and AI music-editing software. The AI can generate whole instrumental tracks or short snippets from text prompts. Parker says an upcoming update will let users hum a melody or beatbox a drum pattern to steer it. items.t: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents
items.d: Apple says it will add new controls around macOS’s Full Disk Access permission, warning that increasingly capable AI agents make broad access to users’ files, messages, mail, and browsing history riskier.
items.fullText: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS. The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said. Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages. The decision also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data. AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings. In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history. “Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers. The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.” “Addressing this is critical. items.d: The bill aims to prevent data centers from spiking local utility costs. Republicans accused Democrats of playing political games, noting the bill passed the House 417-3.
items.fullText: Artificial intelligence Senate Democrats block Husted-led bill on data centers, calling it ‘toothless’ The bill aims to prevent data centers from spiking local utility costs. Republicans accused Democrats of playing political games, noting the bill passed the House 417-3. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images file Share Add NBC News to Google Sept. 30, 2026, 1:41 PM EDT By Sahil Kapur WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities. The vote was 57-43, short of the 60 needed to break a filibuster. The Ratepayer Protection Act , which passed the House by a vote of 417-3 two weeks ago, would set a federal standard on the issue. It would also instruct state public utility commissions to find ways to make developers of data centers that use huge amounts of energy cover their own costs of water and electricity to consumers. The Senate version is led by appointed Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who’s locked in a competitive battle as he seeks his first full Senate term. He is facing heat at home from Democratic rival Sherrod Brown, a former senator who has branded him “the face of data centers” for promoting developments when he was lieutenant governor. “I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices,” Husted said of Democrats on Tuesday. “All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president’s desk, and we will have a bipartisan win.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the bill would be merely “optional” for states and wouldn’t achieve much beyond partisan messaging for Republicans. “Plain and simple, the Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill.

items.fullText: 판타지의 경계를 확장하다: 삼성 스페이셜 사이니지가 도쿄게임쇼 2026에서 펼치는 캐릭터 IP와 리테일의 미래 2026/09/23 AI 요약 새로운 뉴스룸 AI 기능을 살펴보세요! 닫기 --> AUDIO Play Download 공유 레이어 열기 인쇄하기 9월 17일부터 20일까지 일본 지바현 마쿠하리 멧세(Makuhari Messe)에서 열린 도쿄게임쇼 2026(Tokyo Game Show 2026, TGS). 글로벌 게임 기업 엔씨 부스는 게임 속 캐릭터를 눈앞에서 만나는 듯한 경험을 하려는 관람객들의 발길이 이어졌다. 그 중심에는 게임의 세계관을 화면 밖으로 확장한 삼성전자의 무안경 3D 디스플레이 ‘스페이셜 사이니지(Spatial Signage)’가 있었다. 이번 행사에서 엔씨가 선보인 ‘아스트라에 오라티오(Astrae Oratio)’는 마법이 일상에 스며든 판타지 세계를 배경으로 한 신전기 서브컬처 RPG다. 삼성 스페이셜 사이니지는 독자적인 ‘3D 플레이트(3D Plate)’ 기술을 적용해 별도의 3D 안경 없이도 콘텐츠에 생생한 입체감을 선사하며, 게임 속 캐릭터와 세계관을 오프라인 전시 공간으로 확장했다. 팬덤 경험 확장… 캐릭터와의 만남을 현실 공간으로 게임 퍼블리셔와 콘텐츠 IP(Intellectual Property, 지식재산권) 보유 기업에게 오프라인 공간은 디지털 콘텐츠를 현실로 가져오는 중요한 접점이다. 엔씨는 도쿄게임쇼에서 85형과 32형 스페이셜 사이니지를 부스 입구와 대기 공간 등에 배치해 관람객이 이동하는 과정에서도 게임 속 캐릭터와 세계관을 자연스럽게 경험하도록 했다. 부스 입구에는 85형 스페이셜 사이니지로 ‘아스트라에 오라티오’ 게임의 주요 배경인 ‘특구청’ 건물 내 엘리베이터를 재현했다. 대형 디스플레이를 통해 캐릭터를 실제 사람과 가까운 크기로 표현해, 마치 게임 속 등장인물들이 현실 세계에 인사를 건네는 듯한 장면을 연출했다. ▲ ‘아스트라에 오라티오’ 부스 입구에 설치한 85형 스페이셜 사이니지는 게임 속 다양한 캐릭터가 눈 앞으로 다가오는 듯한 연출로 관람객의 이목을 끌었다. 엔씨 아스트라에 오라티오 사업실 이용수 실장은 “관람객들이 부스에 들어서는 순간부터 실제 크기의 캐릭터와 마주하고 게임 세계에 몰입하길 바랐다”면서 “서브컬처 장르에서는 캐릭터의 생동감과 현실감이 특히 중요한데, 스페이셜 사이니지가 이런 특성을 관람객에게 효과적으로 전달할 수 있다고 판단했다”고 말했다. 현장을 찾은 관람객들은 스페이셜 사이니지가 구현한 캐릭터의 크기와 입체감에 주목했다. 콘텐츠 크리에이터 카와이 코코(Kawaii CoCo) 씨는 “캐릭터가 실제로 움직이며 상호작용하는 것처럼 생생하게 느껴졌다”며 “일반 디스플레이보다 훨씬 눈에 띄고 소셜미디어에서도 근사하게 보일 것 같아, 이 장면을 촬영해 제 구독자들에게 소개하고 싶다”고 말했다. ▲ 콘텐츠 크리에이터 카와이 코코 씨는 캐릭터의 움직임이 스페이셜 사이니지를 통해 생동감 있게 전달되어 아스트라에 오라티오 부스로 눈길이 갔다고 말했다. 스페이셜 사이니지는 52mm 1 의 얇은 두께에도 불구하고 마치 화면 뒤에 별도의 공간이 있는 듯한 깊이감을 구현한 것이 특징이다. 이러한 경험은 대중에게 게임과 캐릭터의 첫인상을 전달하는 데도 효과적으로 활용될 수 있다. 관람객 다니엘 아세로(Daniel Acero) 씨는 “처음 봤을 때 스크린 화면인 줄 전혀 몰랐고, 투명한 설치물이라고 생각했다”면서 “마치 화면 뒤에 실제 공간이 있는 것처럼 깊이감이 느껴져서 놀라웠고, 이러한 방식으로 게임 캐릭터를 소개하면 게임에 대한 관심을 높이고 캐릭터의 개성을 효과적으로 전달할 수 있을 것”이라고 말했다. 관람객 동선과 대기 공간에는 32형 스페이셜 사이니지가 설치돼 부스 전반으로 캐릭터 경험을 확장했다. 32형 제품은 49.4mm의 얇은 두께로 좁은 공간에도 유연하게 설치가 가능해, 게임 체험을 기다리는 관람객을 대상으로 캐릭터와 세계관에 대한 몰입도를 유지했다. 관람객 토마스 포르티에(Tomas As AI becomes more capable, the industry must accelerate security engineering, broaden access to defensive tools and share what works faster. Technology Changes, Security Fundamentals Endure The internet and cloud computing changed how software operates, while core security responsibilities endured: establish identity, control access, limit exposure and verify that protections work. AI agents introduce new capabilities — reasoning , using tools and adapting actions based on the data they encounter. Those capabilities require applying established principles to new operating conditions. This pace creates pressure. Organizations want the productivity benefits of AI while the practices to govern and secure these systems are still developing. Security Depends on the Full Agent Stack Applications depend on code, data, identities, services and infrastructure. Security depends on how those components work together — and AI agents extend that system . Models provide capabilities; harnesses organize context, tools and workflows; and runtime environments provide the infrastructure within which actions execute. Each part of that stack carries security responsibilities, and proper protection requires controls across each layer, as data, instructions and actions move through the system.
